title: Fourier cutoff for linear threshold functions
statement: There is a real constant $B\ge1$ such that, for every natural number $n$ and every function $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$ taking only the values $-1$ and $1$ and admitting a degree-at-most-one polynomial threshold representation, the following holds for every $\varepsilon$ with $0<\varepsilon\le\tfrac12$: there is a natural number $k$ such that $k\le B/\varepsilon^2$ and the Fourier weight on levels strictly above $k$ is at most $\varepsilon$.
hypotheses_covered: There exists a real constant $B$ with $B\ge1$
$f$ is a real-valued function on the $n$-dimensional Boolean cube
$f$ admits a polynomial threshold representation of degree at most one
replaced: There exists an absolute $B\ge1$ such that for every linear threshold function $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$ and $0<\varepsilon\le1/2$, there is $k\in\mathbb N$ with $k\le B/\varepsilon^2$ and $\sum_{|S|>k}\widehat f(S)^2\le\varepsilon$ under the uniform cube law.
